public_sources.title: Liu, Wu, Summa & Zheng, Adaptive Multilevel Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo for Rare Events Estimation in Language Models
observed_results: For standard direct positive-sample acquisition, the idealized analysis gives Theta(log(1/delta)/p*) samples to obtain a positive response with high probability. Under ideal multilevel proposals it gives O(log(1/p*)[log log(1/p*)+log(1/delta)+1]), changing the rare-event dependence from inverse to polylogarithmic. Under imperfect learned proposals, the polylogarithmic advantage is retained in the theorem when proposal total-variation error remains below the per-level target fraction rho.

On the TinyStories toxic-story task, the paper says brute-force estimation of an event around 1e-5 can require nearly 1e6 samples. Its experiments use 10,240 training samples plus 4,096 evaluation samples for learned methods versus a 1,048,576-response Monte Carlo reference. At the hardest gamma*=7 ablation, p_MC=3.81e-6; with 1,024 samples per level the proposed method reports p_hat=4.89e-6 +/-4.47e-7 and 28.3% relative error. In the main table, standard Twisted SMC reaches zero hit rate/zero estimate and 100% error at the rarest settings while the multilevel method maintains substantial hit rates/ESS.

The multilevel example maintains a substantial positive-sample rate through intermediate levels and reports a final-target positive-sample rate close to 0.3 where direct Twisted SMC has almost zero positive-sample rate.

On StrongREJECT jailbreak rare-event estimation, several standard SMC cells give zero estimates or 100% relative error while the multilevel method often yields single-digit or low-double-digit errors. Example: violence/Llama-3B has p_MC=1.70e-3; standard SMC reports zero and 100% error while the proposed method reports 1.71e-3 and 0.487% error. Training-resource tables report proposed-method time comparable to standard SMC: 50.12 vs 50.83 minutes for Llama-3B, 103.08 vs 109.27 for Llama-8B, and 102.39 vs 108.63 for Qwen-7B, averaged across prompts/seeds.

With an imperfect proxy score, the paper explicitly distinguishes the practical-score rare event from ground truth, derives score-mismatch bounds, and reports substantially better empirical CI coverage than standard Twisted SMC in its tested cases rather than claiming the proxy is ground truth.

public_sources.title: Budde et al., Analysis of non-Markovian repairable fault trees through rare event simulation
observed_results: Across 27 highly resilient repairable non-Markovian dynamic fault trees from seven case studies, methods are compared at fixed runtime using confidence-interval width, convergence/non-null estimate rate and variability.

Automatic importance splitting can dramatically beat crude Monte Carlo as events become rarer. In one HECS5 case, Fixed Effort yields confidence intervals approximately 100 times narrower than CMC at the same runtime.

The study exposes severe regime-specific failures. One Expected Success threshold selected a splitting value 2234 while normal values were seldom above 200 and never above 400, causing oversampling and no confidence interval within 30 minutes.

Fixed Effort can be brittle in high-voltage-cabinet models because repairs are much faster than failures: one failed intermediate region resets the chained estimate. With 90/300-second runs this produced null estimates. The authors connect this to importance functions that ignore time/clock values.

public_sources.title: Peherstorfer, Willcox & Gunzburger, Optimal Model Management for Multifidelity Monte Carlo Estimation
public_sources.source_status: peer-reviewed SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing
observed_results: Optimally allocates an arbitrary collection of surrogate and high-fidelity model evaluations under cost/error information rather than requiring a strict fidelity hierarchy.
Occasional high-fidelity recourse keeps the estimator unbiased for the high-fidelity statistic even without surrogate error bounds or error estimators.
Linear and nonlinear numerical examples report speedups by orders of magnitude over single-model Monte Carlo.

derived_results.claim: The abstract AMS idea from r104 now has a direct LLM-evaluation analogue. Instead of learning an importance/twist proposal against an event so rare that positive examples are initially absent, construct nested score events with a controlled retained fraction, learn a proposal at the easier event, importance-correct its samples while learning the next proposal, and progressively approach the final unsafe-event threshold. Under ideal/proposal-error assumptions this changes positive-sample dependence from inverse in p* to polylogarithmic, while current experiments show large practical reductions in zero-hit failure for rare LLM behaviors.
derived_results.status: strong recent external evidence; preprint and adaptation-specific scope retained

derived_results.claim: The fault-tree and LLM evidence jointly strengthen a failure condition already visible in generic AMS: the progress score/reaction coordinate is not a harmless implementation detail. Poor or structurally incomplete scores can produce catastrophic oversampling, undersampling, or zero estimates. Therefore any adaptation should measure score quality and level-transition health explicitly, include reset/oversampling diagnostics, and keep probability correction separate from score ranking.
derived_results.status: cross-domain synthesis supported by independent system-reliability and LLM rare-event sources

derived_results.claim: For ultra-rare trajectory failures, direct or multilevel importance/splitting methods should be considered before average-metric multifidelity Monte Carlo. For smooth expectations, use low-fidelity models as control variates/model-management resources while retaining explicit high-fidelity correction. The two mechanisms solve different variance problems and should not be merged into one proxy score or one claimed speedup.
derived_results.status: derived routing hypothesis; not locally tested

negative_or_scope_evidence: The 2026 LLM result is a new arXiv v1 preprint, not peer-reviewed evidence. Its theoretical polylogarithmic positive-sample result is idealized and depends on per-level proposal quality; it does not prove an equivalent end-to-end runtime complexity for learned twists.

Rare-event score/evaluator error changes the operational event being estimated. Importance correction fixes proposal sampling bias, not semantic misclassification by the score itself; the paper treats this separately.

The StrongREJECT and toxic-story numbers are tied to the tested prompts, thresholds, evaluators, model families, training budgets and reference estimates. Do not generalize the reported relative errors to all LLM safety evaluations.

The fault-tree 100x CI-width result is a case-specific best example, not a universal splitting factor. The same study contains severe splitting failures when threshold/importance geometry mismatches the failure-repair dynamics.

Multifidelity Monte Carlo orders-of-magnitude speedups require useful correlation/coupling and cost ratios; high-fidelity recourse preserves unbiasedness but does not guarantee variance reduction when surrogates are poor.
None of these results establishes AGI capability improvement; they concern evaluation/simulation efficiency and rare-event observability.

candidate_update.rare_event: Upgrade r104 adaptive rare-event ladder from finance-heavy external evidence to direct LLM-safety plus formal-system-reliability evidence. Preserve the need for a calibrated/corrected estimator and score-quality diagnostics.
candidate_update.multifidelity: Upgrade r104 multilevel-evaluation candidate with arbitrary-surrogate optimal model management and explicit unbiased high-fidelity recourse; still separate from rare-event splitting.

frontier: Inspect the 2026 LLM preprint's ablations for threshold fraction rho, score imperfection, training/evaluation sample allocation and proposal degeneracy; extract conditions where multilevel twist learning becomes worse or unstable rather than only best cases.

Find a rare-event method for interactive or multi-turn agent trajectories where state can be cloned/replayed, and compare to independent episode sampling under a matched probability-estimation or failure-discovery objective.

Find multifidelity/control-variate evidence using learned evaluators or simulators closer to ML systems, with reported correlation/cost ratios and cost-normalized variance reduction, not only PDE/physics surrogates.

Design an adaptation test that keeps score ranking, sampling proposal, and probability estimator as three separate objects so failure of the learned score cannot silently masquerade as improved rare-event probability estimation.
exact_next_action: Continue from the LLM rare-event paper rather than generic AMS. Extract the rho/sample-budget ablations and imperfect-score results into a compact failure-envelope, then search for multi-turn/agent rare-event estimation with replayable state. In parallel identify one learned-evaluator multifidelity Monte Carlo/control-variate study with explicit cost-normalized variance factors. Do not promote a local adaptation until score semantics and probability correction are separately testable.
